=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s assessment

**Do not accept the Seller’s package as settled.** Its combined effect is to transfer known completion risks to Wattlebridge while restricting recovery for both known and undiscovered problems.

The Seller’s “[STANDARD]” labels and “reviewer efficiency note” are not evidence of Buyer agreement. All provisions remain reviewable. Likewise, disclosure of a risk does not resolve it or establish that the proposed contractual protection is adequate.

This assessment is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter, not the complete SPA or underlying DD documents. The final drafting must be checked against those documents.

## 1. Completion protections and price mechanics

### Bluefen: consent alone may not protect the revenue

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The Disclosure Letter acknowledges that neither final consent nor satisfaction of associated conditions has been evidenced. A reasonable-endeavours obligation is not a substitute for an effective completion condition.

**Push back:**
- Require valid written consent **and satisfaction of the applicable clause 11.3 conditions** before Completion.
- Require consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer, without adverse changes to pricing, termination rights or other material commercial terms.
- Make waiver a Buyer decision, with appropriate long-stop and termination rights if the condition fails.

**Reason:** A consent letter could be conditional or commercially damaging. The Seller’s proposed delivery-only test does not establish that the relationship will continue on the expected terms.

### Riverlark: no unsecured promise of release after Completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. Post-Completion release is inconsistent with delivering a debt-free business free of the lender’s security.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a lender payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and discharge costs.
- Pay the lender directly through the completion funds flow, reducing Seller proceeds consistently with the agreed price mechanics.
- Require effective discharge of security and release of relevant guarantees at Completion, supported by binding lender undertakings and controlled registration mechanics where necessary.

**Reason:** The Buyer should not acquire a company still exposed to the Seller’s financing arrangements or rely on the Seller to procure release after receiving the price. Avoid double-counting any repayment already reflected in the price adjustment.

### Completion bonuses: allocate the full cost expressly

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional on Completion and continued employment, and omitted from the draft funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not stop the Company becoming liable.

**Push back:**
- Allocate the bonuses expressly to the Seller economically, through payment, a price deduction or an appropriately secured indemnity.
- Establish payment dates, employment conditions and any payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs.
- Include the agreed treatment in the completion accounts definitions and funds flow, without double recovery.

**Reason:** These are transaction-linked liabilities, not costs the Buyer should inadvertently fund in addition to the agreed price.

## 2. Known risks need specific protection

### Ironquay: payment exposure is not the whole IP risk

The disclosed contractual condition links transfer of SOW3 Project Materials to payment of **every SOW3 fee**. The ledger records AUD 180,000 open, but does not independently prove non-payment. Equally, the data room contains no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Push back:**
- Verify the full payment position and the affected materials.
- Require evidence of cleared payment and, where necessary, an effective confirmatory assignment or other documentation establishing the Company’s rights.
- Expand protection beyond the particular invoice to losses arising from any failure to obtain the relevant IP rights, including appropriate remediation and third-party claim costs.
- If unresolved at Completion, seek a retention or escrow and a specific indemnity outside the general warranty limitations.

**Reason:** Paying AUD 180,000 may not alone establish complete ownership or cure every contractual defect. The business needs usable IP rights, not merely reimbursement of a bill.

### Export/privacy incident: unresolved, not established as immaterial

The disclosure establishes delivery of a download link to an unintended address and potentially approximately 1,240 records. It does **not** establish access, the precise scope, a legally notifiable breach or a loss amount.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation, containment, preservation of evidence and reporting to the Buyer.
- Establish access logs, link permissions, affected information, recipients and applicable privacy and contractual obligations.
- Require legally necessary notifications and remediation, with appropriate Buyer consultation.
- Seek a specific indemnity for losses attributable to the pre-Completion incident, including reasonable investigation, remediation and third-party liabilities, subject to applicable law.

**Reason:** Uncertainty is not evidence of immateriality. Conversely, the Buyer should not assert that a confirmed reportable breach has occurred on this record. If the investigation reveals material exposure, reconsider completion protection and pricing.

### Supplier renewals: investigate before classifying

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither their ordinary-course nature nor their treatment as debt-like liabilities is established.

**Push back:** Review DD-008 and DD-011 together for timing, scope, termination rights, accruals, prepayments and commercial necessity. Restrict new commitments before Completion where appropriate, then agree treatment under the working-capital/debt definitions.

**Reason:** Related commitments should be assessed together, but future operating expenditure is not automatically a Seller deduction.

## 3. The liability package is too broad

### General cap, thresholds and deadline

The proposed **AUD 4.8 million cap**, **AUD 25,000 de minimis**, **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** and **18-month notice period** materially constrain recovery when combined.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher general cap and lower thresholds, calibrated to diligence findings and available security.
- Prefer a tipping basket rather than recovery only above AUD 250,000.
- Aggregate related claims to prevent fragmentation below the de minimis.
- Seek a longer general warranty period covering sufficient reporting cycles.
- Check claim-notice requirements and any separate deadline to commence proceedings; preserve properly notified contingent claims.

**Reason:** Individual limitations cannot sensibly be assessed in isolation from the disclosures, exclusions and remedy restrictions.

### Fundamental, tax and IP protection should not simply follow the general regime

“Administrative simplicity” is no justification for limiting capacity and title claims to 20% of the price for 18 months.

**Push back:**
- Give title, capacity and authority warranties separate protection, ordinarily with recovery up to at least the full purchase price and a materially longer claim period.
- Obtain a dedicated tax covenant/indemnity for pre-Completion taxes, with suitable assessment-period-based timing and separate limitations.
- Assess broader IP warranties and bespoke protection against the business’s dependence on its IP; preserve the specific Ironquay protection.
- Include appropriate fraud and deliberate-concealment carve-outs, with careful attribution drafting.

**Reason:** Failure to acquire the promised shares, historic tax exposure and defective core IP present different risks from ordinary business warranties.

### “All Claims” wording threatens the entire protection package

The proposed application of limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to **all Claims of any nature** could restrict specific indemnities, payment obligations and other contractual remedies—not merely warranty claims.

**Push back:** Confine each limitation to expressly identified claim categories. Preserve agreed indemnities, debt and price-adjustment obligations, completion obligations, equitable relief and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review non-reliance wording carefully and preserve relevant express representations.

**Reason:** A bespoke protection is ineffective if a general clause silently caps or extinguishes it.

## 4. Disclosure and knowledge provisions undermine recourse

Blanket disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room or public records is too broad. The knowledge clause goes further by treating matters merely **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers as known.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter.
- Reject disclosure by remote reference or indiscriminate document dumping.
- Freeze and retain an identifiable data-room archive; control any subsequent disclosures.
- Reject constructive knowledge and automatic attribution of all adviser knowledge. If a knowledge exclusion is conceded, narrowly define actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals.
- State expressly that disclosed matters do not qualify specific indemnities, completion conditions or price obligations unless specifically agreed.

**Reason:** Disclosure may qualify a warranty; it does not repay debt, transfer IP or satisfy consent conditions.

## 5. Avoid unsupported consent and title conclusions

- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies a notification obligation, not landlord consent. Require timely compliance and evidence, but do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not itself require consent to a share sale. Check the complete agreement for separate change-of-control provisions.
- **Share title:** The register is relevant evidence, not comprehensive verification. Check share issuance and transfers, all issued securities and rights to acquire them, encumbrances, transfer restrictions and required approvals. Obtain effective transfers and robust title warranties.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure Completion:** effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark payout and releases; reliable title and IP delivery.
2. **Fix the economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs; verify renewal treatment; reconcile everything through the funds flow without double-counting.
3. **Ring-fence known exposures:** broader Ironquay protection and evidence-led incident investigation, backed by suitable indemnities and security.
4. **Rebuild recourse:** separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; improve general limits; narrow “all Claims” restrictions.
5. **Reject blanket risk transfer:** fair disclosure, no “discoverable knowledge” exclusion, and no assumption that Seller-labelled provisions were agreed.

**Bottom line:** Do not complete against promises to resolve material issues later, and do not let disclosure plus universal limitations leave the Buyer paying for risks the Seller should discharge or retain.
